summary: A proposal from BBN to add a way to resynchronize the status of a single connection in the ARPANET Host-Host protocol. Without it, a lost or corrupted control message could leave the two ends confused, for example the lost allocate and half-closed problems, and the only fix was to reset every connection between two hosts. It was answered in RFC 492.

plainLanguage.summary: When two computers disagreed about whether a connection was still open, the only fix was to reset every connection between them. This 1973 proposal adds a way to repair just the affected connection, and to close the one end of a half-closed connection.

subtitle: A proposal to repair a single ARPANET connection whose two ends disagree, without resetting all connections.

tldr.problem: If a host was interrupted or a control message was lost, the two ends of a connection disagreed about its state, and the Host-Host protocol had no way to repair only that connection.
tldr.mechanism: Two new commands, RCS (reset connection by sender) and RCR (reset connection by receiver), zero the allocation counters at both ends, and the meanings of RTS, STR and ERR are changed so half-closed connections get closed.
tldr.outcome: The authors argue the data stream is preserved, so resynchronizing is safe at any time, and the protocol would become far more robust.

today: The unit metadata records the status of RFC 467 as Unknown, and it is updated by RFC 492. It is a 1973 proposal for the Host-Host protocol.

sections.title: The Problem: Inconsistent Connection State
sections.content:
The Host-Host protocol had no provision for resynchronizing the status information kept at the two ends of a connection. After a service interruption, or a control message lost or corrupted in an interface or in the subnet, the two NCPs stay confused forever.

One symptom is the lost allocate: the receiving NCP believes bit and message allocations are outstanding, while the sending NCP believes it has none, so information flow over that connection can never restart. The RST command is inappropriate because it destroys all connections between the two hosts. The other symptom is the half-closed connection, where one NCP believes the connection is open and the other believes it is closed; the open end should then be closed.
sections.plainLanguage: Two computers can end up disagreeing about whether a connection is still open. Before this proposal the only way to fix that was to hang up every connection between them, which threw away working traffic.

sections.title: The RCS and RCR Commands
sections.content:
Two new commands are proposed, each an 8-bit command code followed by an 8-bit link field. RCS (reset connection by sender) is sent from the host sending on the link to the host receiving on it. RCR (reset connection by receiver) is sent the other way. A sender might use RCS after a timeout when there is traffic to move but no allocation, or when an inconsistent event occurs, such as an outstanding allocation in excess of 2^32 bits or 2^16 messages.

Resynchronizing means emptying messages and allocates from the pipeline, zeroing the bit and message allocation variables at both ends, and restarting the normal allocate and message exchange. Because RCS and RCR work as a positive acknowledgement pair, the scheme is race-free.
sections.plainLanguage: Two new commands, one for each side, let either end say: forget the old counts and start again from zero. Because each command acts as the other's reply, the two ends cannot get out of step.

sections.title: Sender, Receiver and Simultaneous Resynchronization
sections.content:
To start, the sending NCP enters a waiting-for-RCR-reply state, waits until a RFNM has been received for every regular message sent over the connection, then sends RCS. The receiving NCP zeros its allocation variables, returns to the state ready to accept a message, replies with RCR, and may send an ALL command for any allocation it wants. On receiving the RCR reply, the sending host zeros its variables and becomes ready to send messages.

The receiving NCP may also trigger the same sequence by sending RCR, for example when a TIP or TELNET user expects output but receives none. The sending NCP waits for its pipeline to empty, zeros its variables, and answers with RCS.

If both ends start at once, the RCS and RCR commands cross in the pipeline and each end interprets the other's command as the confirmation reply, so resynchronization happens correctly regardless of timing.
sections.plainLanguage: Either side can start the reset. The other waits until all messages already in flight have been acknowledged, agrees, and both begin fresh. If both start at the same moment, each simply reads the other's command as the agreement.

sections.title: Half-Closed Connections
sections.content:
A longer interruption can leave one end believing the connection is open and the other believing it is closed, perhaps because a user unilaterally dissolved the connection by sending CLS and closing without the acknowledgement, which is legal only if the subnet indicates the destination is dead. The proposal changes the meaning of three existing commands rather than adding new ones.

If the open end keeps sending messages or control messages for its link, the closed end replies with an ERR saying the link is unknown (error code 5). On receiving that ERR, the open end closes the connection in its tables without sending any CLS. If instead the closed end sends an RTS or STR naming the same foreign socket as an existing open connection, the open end closes the old connection first, again without CLS, and then responds.
sections.plainLanguage: When one end finds that the other treats the connection as closed, the reply tells the open end to close it too, so both agree again. No new command is needed for this; three existing commands are given new meanings.
